The holiest shrine of the Sikhs, at Amritsar in the Punjab: a gilded temple in the middle of a square pool, reached by a causeway. It was built by Guru Arjan, the fifth Sikh Guru, and in 1604 he placed in it the Adi Granth, the Sikh scripture.

Its form carries the teaching of Guru Nanak. It has a door on each of its four sides, open to people of every caste and faith, and it stands lower than the ground around it, so that everyone steps down to enter. Its free kitchen, the langar, feeds tens of thousands of people a day, all seated together on the floor.

Afghan armies destroyed it more than once in the 1700s and the Sikhs rebuilt it each time. Ranjit Singh, ruler of the Sikh Empire, covered the upper floors in gold leaf in the early 1800s, which gave it its English name. In 1984 the Indian army stormed the complex to remove armed militants, with heavy loss of life.
